extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, students of Romantic poetry, and editors/critics interested in Coleridge and contemporary journalistic practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative standards from a literary-biographical supplement discussing what makes good poetry, dramatic verse, and newspaper writing (e.g., versification, feeling vs plot, delivery, freshness, regularity). Useful for judging or producing literary and journalistic work in the Romantic period style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facility fatal to excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: "He wrote, indeed, pleasing verse and with plea. facility,—a facility fatal to excellence;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too-ready facility or facility of production in verse is presented as an artistic defect: pleasing ease and fluency can undermine true excellence. Implicit anti-pattern: verse that is produced with excessive ease rather than rigorous craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of analysis / discriminating distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: "his mind was chiefly remarkable for the fine power of analysis which distinguishes his ... later compositions. In this power of discriminating and distinguishing — carried to a pitch almost of painfulness — Lloyd has scarcely ever been equalled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued trait: careful analytical discrimination in thought and description. Works that show subtle, penetrating analysis of manners and minor social nuance are praised; this power can be a primary merit even when other formal elements are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requires calm attention to appreciate
rubrics_metrics.description: "his poems, though rugged in point of versification, will be (bond by those who will read them with the calm attention they require, replete with critical and moral suggestions of the highest value."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems may demand sustained, calm reading to reveal their value. Evaluation should account for cognitive demands placed on readers: lack of immediate polish can be offset by depth discoverable under careful study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification: ease, harmony, and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: "the want of ease and harmony in the flow of the verse is a prevailing defect in Mr. Lloyd's poetry, and often makes it appear prosaic, even where the thought is not so."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical prosody matters: awkward or rugged versification can render thought prosaic. Criterion: smoothness and musicality of line flow; anti-pattern: verse with interesting ideas but halting or prosaic meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineation of character and state of mind in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding The Duke d'Ormond: "great merit as a dramatic poem, in the delineation of character and state of mind; the plot is forced and unnatural; not only that, but... it is tediously subjective; and we feel the actions of the piece to be improbable while the feelings are true to nature; yet there is tragic effect in the scenes of the denouement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating dramatic poetry, distinguish between fidelity of inner feeling (state of mind) and plausibility of action/plot. A work may be meritorious for psychological insight even if its plot is contrived; strong denouement can still produce tragic effect despite improbabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of feeling vs plausibility of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted evaluation: "the actions of the piece to be improbable while the feelings are true to nature; yet there is tragic effect in the scenes of the denouement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: prioritize natural, convincing emotional truth even where external actions strain credulity; judge whether feelings compensate for plot weaknesses and whether emotional truth produces overall dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness of effect for newspaper writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Freshness of effect belongs to a newspaper, and distinguishes it from a literary book... A newspaper is a market for flowers and vegetables, rather than a granary or conservatory;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper prose should aim for immediacy and topical freshness rather than enduring, heavily reworked material. Medium-suitability: ephemeral impact is a key virtue for daily press; pieces intended for newspapers should be judged by freshness more than permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of piece type to medium (newspaper vs pamphlet/book)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prose writing I never expected from him at that time... On those to Judge Fletcher, and many other such essays, as being rather fit for pamphlets than newspapers..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a piece's scope and depth fit the intended medium. Long, discursive, or reflective essays may be better suited to pamphlets/books; newspapers require brevity, topicality, and a format that serves immediate public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and capacity for daily production
rubrics_metrics.description: "Could Coleridge and I place ourselves thirty-eight years back, and be so far a man of business as to write three or four hours a day... To write the leading paragraph of a newspaper I would prefer him to Mackintosh, Burke... but when Coleridge wrote in his study without being pressed, he wandered, and lost himself. He should always have had the printer's devil at his elbow with 'Sir, the printers want copy.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For newspaper employment, consistent daily output and adherence to editorial deadlines are essential. Brilliant occasional pieces are insufficient if the writer cannot reliably produce copy on schedule; productivity and discipline are evaluative criteria for journalistic suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of minute, picturesque, lively accounts for newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have known the Paper served more by a minute, picturesque, lively account of the ascension of a balloon than ever it was by any piece of writing... There is a great difference among newspapers in this respect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, vivid, and picturesque reporting of events can have larger impact on readership than abstract or high literary writing. Criterion: immediacy, sensory detail, and liveliness increase a report's value to a newspaper audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unremitting attention to early and full accounts raises newspaper success
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was unremitting attention and success in giving the best and earliest accounts of occurrences that made The Morning Post..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial strategy matters: prioritizing earliest, fullest coverage of events (and useful exclusives) is a primary metric of a paper's success; in evaluation, measure timeliness and comprehensiveness of reporting as key strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial preference: news and short notices over brilliant but long essays
rubrics_metrics.description: "Street always preferring news, and a short notice of it in a leading paragraph, to any writing, however brilliant... little or nothing that he wrote was inserted, from want of room."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may favor concise news-led items over lengthy literary pieces regardless of brilliance. When producing for press, prioritize concise, newsworthy content to match editorial priorities and space constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral delivery/recitation enhances poetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of Coleridge's recitation: "his voice 'rose like a stream of rich distill'd perfume';... recitation ... gave a bewitching effect to its wizard ... his recitation of Kubla Khan..." and "swept... into a continuous strain of eloquent dissertation, certainly the most novel, the most finely illustrated, and traversing the most spacious fields of thought, by transitions the most just and logical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance (voice, pacing, illustrative detail, and transitions) is a criterion of a poem's immediate power. For lyric and dramatic poetry, evaluate not only the written text but also its potential or realized oral delivery: tone, modulation, and logical transitions can amplify reception.
